episodes.title: Episode 05: What a player can know
notes: Determinisation: the teacher deals the unseen cards at random and plays each deal out.
The original sampler kept the opponent's discard pile exactly, which no player ever sees.
The public sampler pools the opponent's draw pile, hand and discard; only Bureaucrat's top cards are public (Harbinger, Artisan, Sentry are private).
Same observation gives identical grades; tested with swaps that keep or change what a player can see.
Of 31 proposed overrides on the bank, 74% hold on its own values; under the public sampler 61% and with an opponent mixture 71%, versus 52% for the original view at 64 draws.
transcript: A search in a card game has a problem that chess does not. You cannot see your opponent's hand, or the order of your own deck. So how can the teacher play a position to the end? This episode is about how it deals with hidden cards, a quiet flaw in how it did that, and the test that checks whether the flaw mattered.

The method is called determinisation. Before each rollout, the teacher fills in everything it cannot see with one random guess that agrees with what it can see. My own draw pile has known contents but an unknown order, so it gets shuffled. The opponent's hidden cards get dealt at random. Then the game is played to the end as if that guess were true. Thirty two rollouts means thirty two guesses. Averaging over the guesses approximates the average over the real uncertainty, as long as each guess is drawn from the right distribution.

Here is the catch: from the right distribution. A guess must only use information a player really has. A simple test captures this. If two game states look identical to the player, the teacher must give them identical grades. To make that exact, the teacher first sorts every hidden zone into a fixed order, and only then shuffles with the seed. Two states that differ only in hidden details then produce the same thirty two deals, card for card.

The reviewer spotted the flaw. The original sampler shuffled the opponent's hand and draw pile together, but it kept the opponent's discard pile exactly as it was. A real player cannot know that. When your opponent ends a turn, the cards left in their hand go to the discard pile face down. You never see them. So the teacher knew slightly more than a player could. It also reshuffled cards that everyone had seen placed on the opponent's deck.

So I built a public view. In it, the opponent's draw pile, hand and discard pile are pooled together and dealt again at their visible sizes. That is pessimistic, because a careful player remembers some of the discard pile. The truth lies between the two views. I also had to work out which cards on top of a deck are public. In this card set only one card makes them public: the Bureaucrat. It puts a Silver on its owner's deck, and it makes the victim put a victory card back, both in plain view. Harbinger, Artisan and Sentry put cards back that only their owner sees. The tracker follows this at every decision. A shuffle makes a pile unknown again. A draw removes the top. And growth of a pile is private exactly when the previous decision was its owner's Harbinger, Artisan or Sentry choice. Tests check all of it. Swapping an opponent's discarded card with a hidden card in their deck gives identical grades in the public view, but different grades in the original view. A public top card is never moved.

There is a second hidden assumption. During a rollout, the opponent is played by its real network. But our network is never told who it plays. A lesson measured against one particular opponent might not hold against another. So the teacher can also play the opponent's side with a fixed mixture: our network, the earlier network, an older champion, and the genetic algorithm player, one after another across the deals.

The test. On the held out bank, the teacher would override our network in thirty one positions. Against the bank's own high precision values, seventy four percent of those still beat our network's choice by more than two points. Then I regraded each one with sixty four fresh deals in four ways. The original view kept fifty two percent. The public view kept sixty one percent. The opponent mixture kept sixty one. And both together kept seventy one. Thirty one positions is a small sample, and sixty four deals is still noisy, so read these as similar, not as an improvement. The important result is that the public view does not undo the teacher's lessons. The teacher was not winning by peeking.
That closes the groundwork. The next episode will be about the race between the two training branches, when it finishes.

episodes.title: Episode 04: Teaching without breaking
notes: Pairwise loss: verified gain x softplus(-(logit_b - logit_c)); slope = logistic(-d), the Bradley-Terry form.
Anchor: KL(frozen c2 || new net) on 84,575 of c2's own positions (all decision kinds) + the win estimate; gradient = new minus frozen probabilities.
lambda 1: 98% of training pairs learnt, anchors broke (buy agreement 72%); one variant scored 21.7% vs c2.
lambda 100: agreement 97%, held-out pairs barely move; dev match 52.5% [49.3, 55.8] (best of 5 settings).
305 training lessons are too few to teach a transferable rule; branch B starts from the lambda-100 net.
transcript: We had three hundred and eighty nine verified lessons. In each one, the teacher found a buy that beats our network's own choice, and confirmed it on fresh deals. This episode is about how to put those lessons into the network, the mathematics of the two forces involved, and what happened when I tried.

The student is our best network itself. That was a deliberate choice. An earlier attempt trained a separate small network from scratch, and it never got past fifty percent. Starting from the network that already plays well, we only need to nudge a few decisions.

The first force is the lesson. For each verified position, call the teacher's buy b and our network's buy c. The network gives each a logit, a score. I want the score of b to rise above the score of c. Write d for the difference, the logit of b minus the logit of c. The loss for that position is the verified gain times the softplus of minus d. Softplus is the logarithm of one plus e to the x. When d is very negative, the loss grows like minus d, a steady push. When d is large and positive, the loss fades to zero. Its slope is the logistic function of minus d. So the push is strongest while c still wins, and it relaxes once b is clearly ahead. This is the same form as the Bradley Terry model for comparing two players. Weighting by the verified gain means a lesson worth twenty points pushes ten times harder than one worth two.

The second force is the anchor. The network makes about two hundred decisions per game: playing actions, buying, trashing, discarding, choosing gains. Only buys were labelled. If I only push on buys, the shared layers move, and every other decision moves with them. So I collected eighty four thousand five hundred positions from our network's own games, of every kind. On each, I compare the new network's probabilities with the frozen network's. The measure is the Kullback Leibler divergence. In words: for each option, take the frozen probability, multiply by the log of the frozen probability over the new probability, and add them up. It is zero when nothing changed, and it grows as the new network disagrees. Its gradient on the logits is simply the new probabilities minus the frozen ones. A second anchor term holds the win estimate in place.
The total loss is the lesson plus lambda times the anchor. Lambda decides who wins the tug of war.

With lambda equal to one, the lessons won. On the training lessons, the network chose the teacher's buy ninety eight percent of the time. But on held out lessons, from kingdoms it never saw, only about a quarter moved. And the anchors broke. On its own positions, the new network agreed with the old one only eighty six percent of the time, and only seventy two percent on buys. With a looser label threshold it was worse. That version scored twenty one point seven percent against the original network. It had memorised three hundred buys and forgotten how to play.

With lambda equal to one hundred, the anchors held. Agreement stayed at ninety seven percent overall, ninety four and a half on buys. The divergence fell to about one hundredth. But now the held out lessons barely moved: about one in twenty. Against the original network, on three hundred fresh development kingdoms, it scored fifty two and a half percent. The interval runs from forty nine point three to fifty five point eight. That was the best of five settings I tried on those kingdoms, so it is flattered a little by selection. Lambda three hundred scored fifty one point six.

What does that mean? Three hundred and five training lessons are too few to teach a rule that transfers. Each one is a rare exception: a particular deck, supply and score where a different buy is better. The network can memorise them, but memorising them costs more elsewhere than it gains. The honest summary is that the supervised step made a small change of uncertain value. On the bank, it changed about seven percent of buys, and their average effect was slightly positive, but tiny.

That is why the next step matters. Both branches now get exactly the same reinforcement training, on the same games. If the small nudge helps, branch B should stay ahead of branch A. If it does not, we will know that too.

episodes.title: Episode 03: Six hundred games, four arms, one build
notes: 300 fresh kingdoms x 2 seats, one frozen build: mirror, buy teacher, action teacher, both.
The mirror scores exactly 50%: a deterministic policy against itself on the same seed plays the same game from both seats.
Intervals: bootstrap over kingdom pairs (4,000 resamples).
Median buy-teacher decision 0.8 s, 95th percentile 2.6 s: why the knowledge must move into the network.
transcript: You might remember earlier numbers for the teacher: fifty nine percent with buy search, and sixty two with buys and actions together. They came from different games, different builds and different days. The handoff asked for something cleaner. All arms on the same games, with the same code, before we build anything on top of them. This episode is about that experiment, and about how to read its intervals.

First, the design. I wrote a frozen list of three hundred fresh kingdoms, each with a seed, before any game was played. None of them appears in any earlier test, and none will ever be used for training. Each kingdom is played twice, once with our teacher in each seat. So every arm plays six hundred games, and all four arms play exactly the same six hundred. I also froze one compiled copy of the teacher, and every match records a fingerprint of that file and of every source file. If anyone resumes a match with different code, it refuses.
The four arms. A mirror: our network against itself, with no search. Then the buy teacher. Then the action teacher, which searches when to play which action card and when to stop. And both together.

The mirror is a nice check. Our network plays its single favourite move, with no randomness. If both seats are the same network on the same seed, the game played from seat one and the game played from seat two are the same game. One copy wins exactly when the other loses. So every kingdom gives exactly one half, and the mirror must score exactly fifty percent, with an interval of zero width. It did. That tells you the pairing is right.

Now the unit of evidence. A single game is not independent of its partner, because the two seats share the kingdom. So the unit is a kingdom pair: the average of the two games. That average can be zero, one quarter, one half, three quarters or one. The score is the mean over three hundred pairs. For the interval I resample the three hundred pairs with replacement four thousand times, recompute the mean each time, and take the middle ninety five percent. That is a bootstrap. It needs no assumption about the shape of the distribution.

The results. The buy teacher scored fifty six percent, with an interval from fifty three to fifty nine. The action teacher scored fifty five point one, from about fifty two and a half to fifty eight. Both together scored fifty eight point eight, from about fifty five and a half to sixty two. Not a single game had an engine error. Between one and four games per arm reached the round limit.

Then the paired differences, which are the real question. Because all arms played the same kingdoms, I can subtract them pair by pair. That removes the variation between kingdoms, just as pairing removed the variation between deals last episode. Buy search minus nothing: six points, from three to nine. Action search minus nothing: about five points. Both minus buy alone: two point eight points, but the interval runs from minus one point two to plus six point seven. So adding action search on top of buy search may help, but this test cannot show it yet.

Speed matters too. The buy teacher's median decision took about point eight seconds, and one in twenty took over two and a half seconds, on a shared laptop. That is far too slow to play like that for real. That is the reason for the whole project: to move what the search knows into the network, where it costs nothing.

The rule for what to label next was written before the results. Take the simplest arm that clearly beats plain play. The buy teacher's interval sits above fifty percent, so the pilot labelled buys only. Next episode: how to teach our network those buys without breaking everything else it knows.

episodes.title: Episode 02: Thirty two futures and the winner's curse
notes: One rollout is a coin flip: standard deviation about 0.5, so 32 rollouts give a standard error of about 9 points.
Pairing: every candidate is played on the same 32 deals; shared luck cancels in the difference.
The gate: override only when the paired gain exceeds 2 points and 2 standard errors (3.9% of buys in the ablation).
Winner's curse: the best of six equal noisy estimates looks about 1.27 standard errors too good; independent validation draws remove it.
Pilot: 20,120 graded buys, 389 verified improvements (1.9%); bank of 1,000 positions at 128-512 draws: c2 loses about 1.7 points per buy.
transcript: The teacher in this project is a search. At a decision, it tries each candidate move, and plays the rest of the game to the end, many times. This episode is about the mathematics of that search. How noisy is it, how do we make it less noisy, and why does choosing the best of several noisy numbers fool you?

Start with one candidate, say buying a Gold. The teacher copies the game. It deals the cards it cannot see at random: the order of its own draw pile, and the opponent's hidden cards. Then our best network plays both sides to the end. A win counts one, a tie one half, a loss zero. That is one rollout. Do it thirty two times, with thirty two different deals, and average. That average estimates the chance of winning after buying Gold.

How precise is that estimate? A single rollout is a coin flip with some probability p. Its standard deviation is the square root of p times one minus p. Near p equals one half, that is one half. Averaging thirty two of them divides the spread by the square root of thirty two, which is about five point seven. So the standard error is about nine percentage points. That is a lot. Two candidates whose true values differ by five points would often swap places.

The first trick is pairing. The teacher plays every candidate on the same thirty two deals. Deal number seven is the same shuffle for Gold, for Laboratory, and for passing. Many deals decide the game almost on their own: a lucky draw wins whatever you bought. Those deals add the same amount to every candidate. When you subtract two candidates deal by deal, that shared luck cancels. The variance of a difference is the sum of the two variances minus twice their covariance. Pairing makes the covariance large, so the difference is much more precise than either value alone.

The second trick is the gate. The teacher only overrides our network when the paired gain is larger than two percentage points, and also larger than two standard errors of that paired difference. Two standard errors is roughly a ninety five percent one sided test. In the matched comparison this gate let the teacher change three point nine percent of buys.

Now the winner's curse. Suppose six candidates are truly equal. Each estimate has noise. If you pick the largest of six noisy numbers, you will almost always pick one whose noise happened to be positive. For six independent normal errors, the expected maximum is about one point two seven standard deviations above the truth. With a standard error of five points, the winner looks about six points better than it is, even when no candidate is better at all. The two standard error gate helps, but a teacher that trains on its own winners would still learn noise.

So every label now has a second, independent test. When the teacher's best candidate is not our network's own choice, it plays that winner and our network's choice again, on thirty two fresh deals it has never used. Only if the winner beats the network's choice there, by more than two points and two standard errors, is the label called verified. Because the fresh deals are independent of the selection, they carry no winner's curse.

What did the pilot give? The teacher graded twenty thousand one hundred and twenty buy decisions. That took four and a half million rollouts and forty seven minutes on seven workers. In thirty seven percent of positions, some candidate looked at least a little better than the network's choice. After verification, only three hundred and eighty nine survived. That is one point nine percent. With a looser test, at one standard error, there were one thousand four hundred and eighty nine.

Then a bank. One thousand held out positions, every legal buy graded again with one hundred and twenty eight fresh deals, and one hundred of them with five hundred and twelve. On the bank, our network loses about one point seven percentage points per buy against the best option. The teacher's shortlist of the top five buys loses less than one tenth of a point. And when the teacher would override, it is clearly right about four times as often as it is clearly wrong.

The picture is consistent. Our network is very good. Its mistakes are rare and small, and measuring them takes hundreds of games per position. Next episode: the matched experiment that tested which kind of search actually wins games.

episodes.title: Episode 01: A ratio that was wrong from the first step
notes: PPO multiplies each lesson by a ratio of new to old probability and clips it to between 0.8 and 1.2.
The C sampler divided logits by the temperature; the PyTorch update did not: at temperature 0.7 the first ratio was off by about 5% and 3.6% of decisions were already clipped.
Invisible at temperature 1, the setting all earlier runs used.
Fixed in one line; a step-zero check now measures the error (about 3e-7) before every run.
Also fixed: errored and overflowed games give no records; seeds instead of run names; two runs with one seed give identical weights.
transcript: This series follows one question. Can a slow search teach our best Dominion network something lasting? Before any of that could run, I had to fix the training itself. This first episode is about one small piece of mathematics, and why a tiny mismatch in it matters.

Our network is trained with an algorithm called proximal policy optimisation. People say P P O. Here is the idea in words. The network plays three thousand games. At every decision it does not simply take its favourite option. It draws an option at random, with a probability for each one. Then, after the games, it asks a question about every decision it made. Did that choice turn out better or worse than expected? Better choices get a higher probability. Worse ones get a lower probability.

The key quantity is a ratio. Take the probability that the new network gives to the move that was played. Divide it by the probability that the old network gave to the same move, at the moment it was played. If the network has not changed, that ratio is exactly one. P P O multiplies each lesson by this ratio. And it clips it. If the ratio wanders outside a band from point eight to one point two, the gradient through that decision stops in one direction. The clip is a safety rail. It keeps each update small.

Now, the probabilities. The network outputs a score for each option, called a logit. To turn scores into probabilities you exponentiate them and divide by their sum. That is the softmax. There is one extra knob, called the temperature. Before the softmax, you divide every logit by the temperature. A temperature below one sharpens the distribution: the favourite gets more likely. A temperature above one flattens it.

Here is the bug. The game engine, written in C, drew moves using the temperature. It recorded the log probability of the move it drew, with the temperature included. But the training code, in PyTorch, computed the new probability without the temperature. So at the very first step, before anything had changed, the two probabilities came from two different softmaxes. The ratio was not one.

How big was the error? The reviewer measured it with our best network's real weights, at a temperature of point seven, on nine hundred and sixty three real decisions. The ratio was off by about five percent on average. And about three and a half percent of all decisions were already outside the clipping band, before a single update. For those decisions the safety rail was engaged for no reason at all.

Why was it never noticed? Because our runs used a temperature of exactly one. Dividing by one changes nothing. The bug only appears at other temperatures. That is a lesson worth keeping. A check that runs only at the default setting cannot find a bug that only lives at the other settings.

The fix is one line. The update now divides the logits by the same temperature as the sampler, and the entropy term uses the same distribution. Then I added a test that plays real games with the real network at temperature point seven and at temperature one. It compares the probability the engine recorded with the probability PyTorch computes. After the fix, the average error is about three parts in ten million. That is just float rounding. Every training run now does this check at step zero, and refuses to start if it fails.

There were other fixes of the same kind. Games the engine reports as broken no longer feed the training. A game whose record buffer overflowed is dropped too, because a truncated game gives wrong credit to the moves before the cut. The random stream that chooses kingdoms and opponents used to depend on the run's name. Now it depends on a seed. And the results come back from the worker processes in a fixed order. Together these mean that two runs with the same seed write identical weights, bit for bit. That matters for everything that follows. When we compare two training branches, the only difference between them must be the one we put there on purpose.
Next episode: how the teacher decides that one move is better than another, and why picking the best of six noisy numbers fools you.
